summaries.example: Think about a chess set. You can count it as one game set, as 33 connected pieces and a board, or as many tiny particles. These are different ways of counting the same thing. Philosophers ask whether the world is one, many, or none under a particular way of counting.
summaries.summary: Monism is the idea of oneness, but philosophers must first explain what is supposed to be one and what counts as a unit. A forest can be counted as one forest or as many trees, so different answers may describe the same scene. The entry focuses on two important views about concrete objects. Existence monism says that exactly one concrete object exists. Priority monism allows many objects, such as people, planets, and particles, but says that the whole world is the one basic object. The smaller things are real but depend on the whole. This makes priority monism different from existence monism, which has trouble accepting ordinary objects as separate concrete things. Philosophers have offered reasons for both monism and pluralism. Some argue that everyday experience shows many objects. Others argue that the world works as one connected system and that a simple account should avoid adding basic things without need. The entry does not present the debate as settled; it surveys arguments and explains why priority monism deserves serious consideration.
key_ideas: Monism can mean different things because philosophers may choose different targets and different counting units.
Existence monism says that exactly one concrete object exists.
Priority monism says that many concrete things may exist, but only one concrete thing—the whole world—is basic.
The SEP entry gives more attention to priority monism because it can accept ordinary objects while saying that the whole is fundamental.
Arguments about monism compare common sense, simplicity, parts and wholes, and ideas from physics.
summaries.why_it_matters: Monism teaches us to ask a careful question before arguing about whether reality is one or many: One what, and counted how? This helps us understand disagreements instead of treating them as simple yes-or-no puzzles. It also raises a lasting question about the relationship between a whole and its parts: Are the parts more fundamental, or does the whole make the parts what they are?

important_terms.definition: The view that something is one, but only after we say what we are counting and how we are counting it.
The view that something is many under a particular way of counting.
The view that there is nothing of the kind being counted.
A way of asking what is most basic or depends on nothing deeper.
A real, physical thing, such as a tree, a person, or a planet.

questions_to_think_about: When you count a forest, are you counting one forest or many trees?
Could many things exist while still depending on one larger whole?
Is a pile of blocks more basic than the pile, or is the pile more basic than the blocks?
Why might a simple explanation be attractive in philosophy?

summaries.example: A mosaic can be described as one artwork, many tiles, or one pattern made from those tiles. Those descriptions do not automatically contradict one another because they use different units of counting. A priority monist makes a metaphysical version of this move: many concrete objects may exist, but the cosmos is the single basic concrete object, while its proper parts are derivative.
summaries.summary: The SEP entry argues that there is no single, unqualified doctrine called monism. A monistic claim must identify a target—such as concrete objects, properties, or categories—and a unit of counting—such as highest types, individual tokens, or basic tokens. The same reality can therefore be one under one description and many under another. The entry concentrates on existence monism and priority monism. Existence monism says that exactly one concrete object exists. This view faces a strong challenge from perception and common sense, which seem to present separate objects. Priority monism makes a weaker and importantly different claim: many concrete objects exist, but exactly one is basic. The cosmos is treated as the fundamental whole, and its proper parts are derivative or dependent on it. Priority pluralism reverses the direction of dependence by treating some parts as fundamental. The dispute is thus about ontological priority rather than simply about what exists. The entry examines arguments on both sides. Support for priority monism includes the possibility of emergent properties in entangled quantum systems, the idea that a world can lack ultimate parts, and the thought that the cosmos forms one integrated causal system. Challenges include the apparent priority of parts in heaps and mosaics, the world’s internal variety, theories of intrinsic properties, and arguments involving possible larger or smaller worlds. The overall conclusion is cautious: no surveyed objection decisively defeats priority monism, and several arguments give it reason for serious reconsideration.
key_ideas: Monism is doubly relative: it depends on the target being counted and the unit used for counting.
Existence monism and priority monism are distinct. The first claims there is one concrete object; the second claims there is one basic concrete object.
Existence monism entails priority monism, but priority monism does not entail existence monism: many derivative objects may exist.
Priority monism treats the maximal whole, normally the cosmos, as prior to its proper parts; priority pluralism instead treats parts as basic.
The debate concerns fundamentality, not necessarily the inventory of ordinary objects. Both sides may accept the world, people, planets, and particles.

Arguments for priority monism appeal to holistic features of quantum systems, the unity of cosmic laws, and the possibility of worlds without ultimate parts; objections appeal to common sense, heterogeneity, intrinsic properties, and modal cases.
summaries.why_it_matters: The debate matters because it concerns what makes an explanation fundamental. If the whole world is basic, then ordinary objects can still exist while depending on a deeper unity. If parts are basic, then wholes may be constructed from more fundamental ingredients. These alternatives affect how we think about explanation, dependence, physical theory, and the meaning of “one” and “many.” Monism also shows why philosophical arguments must state their counting rules rather than relying on an unexplained picture of reality.

important_terms.definition: A thesis of oneness relative to a specified target and unit of counting; it is contrasted with pluralism and nihilism.
The target is what is being counted, while the unit specifies how it is counted; both are needed to state a monistic thesis precisely.
The view that exactly one concrete object token exists, often identified with the whole cosmos.
The view that exactly one concrete object is basic, even though many other concrete objects may exist derivatively.
A relation of dependence in which one entity is fundamental and another exists in virtue of it.
An entity that is not posterior to anything else in the relevant domain; it serves as a foundation for derivative entities.
The view that concrete objects fall under one highest type, such as material, mental, or a neutral type.
The study of parts, wholes, and their relations.

questions_to_think_about: Does counting a forest as one undermine the existence of its trees, or merely use a different unit?
Can a whole be fundamental while its parts remain real and useful for explanation?
Should simplicity favor one basic object, or should an account preserve ordinary objects as distinct?
If quantum entanglement gives a whole information not fixed by its parts, does that support priority of the whole?
Could common sense consistently say that parts are prior in heaps but wholes are prior in integrated systems?

summaries.example: Imagine a school made of classrooms, students, teachers, and shared rules. You can count the school as one institution, many people, or many rooms. These counts can all be useful. A philosopher might ask which of these is most basic. Does the institution depend on the people and rooms, or do the parts depend on the organized school? This resembles the difference between priority pluralism and priority monism.
summaries.summary: Monism is not just the claim that “everything is one.” The entry explains that a philosopher must say what is being counted and what counts as a unit. For example, concrete objects can be counted as individual things, as kinds of things, or as basic things. This produces several different monisms. Substance monism says that all concrete objects belong to one highest type, such as a material or mental type. Existence monism says that only one concrete object exists. Priority monism is different: it says that exactly one concrete object is basic, while many other objects may exist in a dependent way. The basic object is normally understood as the whole cosmos. The central disagreement between priority monism and priority pluralism is therefore about priority—what reality rests on—not simply about whether tables, people, or planets exist. The entry surveys arguments for and against these views. Common experience seems to support many separate objects, especially in ordinary cases such as heaps or mosaics. Yet other cases, such as organized living systems or a connected cosmos, may make the whole seem more fundamental. Discussions of quantum entanglement also raise the possibility that a whole can have features not determined by descriptions of its parts alone. Other objections concern the world’s variety and the nature of intrinsic properties. The entry concludes that priority monism is controversial but not easily dismissed.
key_ideas: There are many kinds of monism because philosophers can count different targets in different ways.
A person can be a monist about one target but a pluralist about another.
Existence monism says there is only one concrete object, while priority monism allows many concrete objects but says only one is fundamental.
Priority monism and priority pluralism may agree about which objects exist and disagree about which objects explain or support the others.
The entry presents arguments rather than a final proof. Some arguments favor the whole; others favor its parts.
Priority monism has received renewed attention because it may combine a unified world with ordinary objects.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic matters because it asks how reality is organized. When something is a whole, do its parts come first, or can the whole be the foundation on which the parts depend? Thinking about this can improve our reasoning about systems, explanations, and scientific pictures of the universe. It also reminds us that a disagreement about “one” and “many” may hide a deeper disagreement about what kind of counting is appropriate.

important_terms.definition: The idea that something is one relative to a chosen target and a chosen way of counting.
The idea that something is many under a chosen target and way of counting.
The target is what is being counted; the unit is the kind of thing used to count it.
The claim that exactly one concrete object exists.
The claim that exactly one concrete object is basic, even if many other objects exist.
The idea that one thing is more fundamental and another depends on it.
The study of how parts and wholes relate.

questions_to_think_about: Can two descriptions of the same scene—one forest and many trees—both be true?
Why is priority monism easier to reconcile with everyday experience than existence monism?
Are the parts of a heap more fundamental than the heap? What about the parts of a living body?
Would a very simple theory always be better than a more familiar theory?
What might it mean for the universe to be one connected system?
